chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from al-Amriki, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), who said:

I asked him about a man who prays on moist, growing grass. He said, 'If he presses his forehead to the ground, there is no harm.' And on thick, growing grass, where it touches fresh earth, he said, 'There is no harm.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn: That some of our companions wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Mazi (peace be upon him) asking him about praying on glass. He said, 'When my letter reached him, he pondered and said,
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray on glass or moist grass in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarates the jurisprudential distinction between natural earth and processed materials, permitting prayer on moist or thick grass provided the forehead makes direct contact with the soil. Conversely, it prohibits prayer on glass by classifying it as 'transformed' (masukh) salt and sand, thereby excluding it from the category of true earth (ard) required for prostration. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the physical purity and natural origin of the prayer surface.
